regions.name: Pfalz
regions.summary: The Pfalz is the warm, dry strip of vineyard that runs north to south along the eastern foot of the Haardt hills, from the Rheinhessen border down to the French frontier at Schweigen, where Alsace begins. It is Germany's second largest region by vineyard and rivals the Mosel for the largest planting of Riesling anywhere in the world. Its heart is the Mittelhaardt, the run of villages around Forst, Deidesheim, Ruppertsberg and Wachenheim that made full, dry Riesling famous. The south, the Südliche Weinstrasse, is warmer again and belongs as much to the Pinot family as to Riesling. Think ripe, dry, broad and spicy, with figs and almonds growing between the rows.

terroir.climate: The Haardt, the northern continuation of the Vosges, wrings the rain out of the westerly weather before it reaches the vines, so the Pfalz sits in a rain shadow. It is one of the driest and sunniest corners of Germany, with mild winters and long, warm summers; figs, almonds, lemons and kiwi fruit grow along the wine road. Riesling ripens fully here in almost every year, which is why the region's natural style is dry. Drought in a hot summer is a greater hazard than rot.
terroir.soils: Weathered sandstone washed down from the Haardt gives the Mittelhaardt its light, warm, free-draining base, mixed with loam, loess and gravel on the lower ground. Limestone surfaces at Deidesheim, Kallstadt and widely across the south. At Forst, black basalt from the Pechsteinkopf outcrop above the village was quarried and spread over the vineyards for generations to darken and warm the soil. In the Südliche Weinstrasse, Birkweiler's Kastanienbusch adds red slate to a palette of loess, loam and shell limestone.
terroir.topography: The vineyards lie on the gentle eastern slopes and foothills where the forested Haardt drops to the Rhine plain, mostly between roughly 100 and 250 metres. The ridge shelters them from the west and the flat plain spreads east towards the Rhine, which is some kilometres away. There is nothing here like the Mosel's cliffs: the best sites are modest slopes at the edge of the forest that catch the morning sun and drain fast.
terroir.water: The Rhine is too far east to shape the vineyards directly, so the Pfalz's water story is the shortage of it: shelter and dryness rather than a river's reflected light.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Fuller and riper than on the Mosel, usually dry, with yellow stone fruit, a spicy, smoky edge on basalt and sandstone, and firm acidity that keeps the weight honest.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: This deeply coloured 1955 Weinsberg crossing is the most planted red grape of the Pfalz: soft, dark-fruited reds from easy quaffers to oaked bottlings.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder from the limestone and red slate of the south, Schweigen and Birkweiler above all, gives some of Germany's most serious dry reds.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder makes dry, creamy, understated whites that suit oak and food, and the VDP admits it to Grosses Gewächs here.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder gives rounder, pear and nut scented dry whites, fuller than the Grigio style of Italy.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Still widely planted for simple, soft, early drinking whites, often sold dry as Rivaner.

grapes.name: Scheurebe
grapes.styles: An aromatic Riesling crossing of grapefruit and blackcurrant leaf, made dry, as Kabinett or as a botrytis sweet wine.

grapes.name: Rieslaner
grapes.styles: A late ripening Silvaner and Riesling crossing with piercing acidity, kept here for taut Auslese and sweeter wines.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: A Pfalz tradition, with ancient Traminer vines surviving at Rhodt; made dry or off-dry and heavily scented.

wines.note: Dry, ripe Riesling of yellow peach, smoke and spice with a firm acid spine. Serve cool rather than cold, and reach for it with pork, roast chicken or anything with a little spice.
The dry top wine of a single classified site, picked at least at Spätlese ripeness and often built to keep for a decade. Forst and Deidesheim are the names a guest will recognise.
Lightly sweet Pfalz Riesling is riper and broader than the Mosel's and less common than it was; it carries chilli and ginger well.
Pfalz Pinot Noir is darker and warmer than the Ahr's, with ripe cherry and spice and real tannin from the limestone sites of the south. A fine partner for duck or lamb.
Dry Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris, creamy and nutty, the region's answer to a guest who wants an unoaked Chardonnay style.
Deep purple, soft and plummy, sometimes with a little residual sugar; the everyday red of the Pfalz and good with grilled sausages.
Botrytised sweet wines from the aromatic crossings, grapefruit and blackcurrant in Scheurebe, steel and apricot in Rieslaner, with acidity that keeps them from cloying.
Grower sparkling wine from Riesling or the Pinot family by the traditional method; the Pfalz is one of its strongholds and serves it as an aperitif.

made.viticulture: Most Pfalz vineyards are gentle enough to work by machine, so this is a region of wire trained vines on flat or sloping ground rather than stake trained cliffs, and the economics are kinder than on the Mosel. The dryness of the rain shadow makes drought and heat the hazards of a warm year, so growers watch canopy shading, pick earlier than their parents did and have been quick to plant Pinot varieties on the warmest ground. Harvest for dry Riesling runs through late September and October, with the sweet Prädikat wines and botrytis selections hanging on into November. Several leading estates farm organically or biodynamically, and old Traminer and Riesling vines are prized. The carting of crushed basalt onto the sandstone at Forst is the region's most quoted piece of soil engineering, a reminder that terroir here includes two centuries of human editing.
made.winemaking: The Pfalz is a dry wine region first. Riesling is fermented to dryness, often in stainless steel but frequently in the big neutral oak casks, the Stückfass and Doppelstück, that the old estates have always used, and the top wines rest on their lees through the winter. Grosses Gewächs bottlings are released the following September or later and are built for the cellar. The Pinot family is handled in the Burgundian way, Spätburgunder with some whole bunches and barriques, Weissburgunder with lees stirring and a little oak. Dornfelder is made soft and fruity for early drinking or, at the serious end, with barrel ageing. Residual sugar survives only where the grower wants it: a sweet Kabinett or Spätlese is a choice here, not a necessity, and the botrytis wines from Scheurebe and Rieslaner are small, deliberate selections. Grower Sekt by the traditional method is a long Mittelhaardt tradition.

law.classification: The Pfalz is one of Germany's thirteen Anbaugebiete, the regions a Qualitätswein or Prädikatswein must name on its label. German law ranks wine first by must weight at harvest, from Qualitätswein through the Prädikat rungs Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein and Trockenbeerenauslese, and that ladder says nothing about sweetness in the glass. The 2021 reform added an origin pyramid, Anbaugebiet, then Region (the old Bereich), then Ort, then Einzellage and the smaller Gewann, and it made Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs protected legal terms for dry single-site wines, with the whole pyramid binding in full from the 2026 vintage. The Pfalz has two Bereiche, Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstrasse in the north and Südliche Weinstrasse in the south. The VDP's private pyramid, Gutswein, Ortswein, Erste Lage and Grosse Lage, sits alongside, and in the Pfalz its Grosses Gewächs is open to Riesling, Weissburgunder and Spätburgunder.
tiers: Wine without geographical indication, the floor of the ladder.
Pfälzer Landwein: the protected geographical indication level, dry or off-dry.
Quality wine from one Anbaugebiet, in this case the Pfalz, with an official test number; enrichment of the must is allowed.
Quality wine with a ripeness attribute, Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese, ranked by must weight at picking and never enriched.

Protected terms for dry wine of protected origin from a named single vineyard: the ordinance caps Erstes Gewächs at 60 hectolitres per hectare, 70 on steep slopes, and holds Grosses Gewächs to a lower cap, hand picking and a later release.
The association's top site class; its dry wine is Grosses Gewächs, in the Pfalz from Riesling, Weissburgunder or Spätburgunder, hand picked and cropped low.
labels: The northern Bereich holding the classic Riesling villages.
The southern Bereich, warmer, with more Pinot varieties and Dornfelder.
The German Wine Road, opened in 1935, running the length of the region from Bockenheim to the gate at Schweigen.
Legally dry: residual sugar at most 4 grams per litre, or up to 9 where the acidity is within 2 grams of the sugar.
Off-dry; feinherb is a customary term rather than a legal one.
A dry wine from a top classified single site; the VDP marks its own with an eagle on the capsule.
A rosé made from one named grape variety, at Qualitätswein level or above.
Grower sparkling wine, traditional method, from the estate's own grapes.
Estate bottled from the estate's own vineyards.
Müller-Thurgau sold dry under its alternative name.

places.name: Mittelhaardt
places.note: The northern Bereich, officially Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstrasse, is the historic core: a line of villages on sandstone, loam and limestone at the foot of the Haardt around Bad Dürkheim and Neustadt. The Bavarian tax survey of 1828 ranked these sites, and the ranking still shapes prices. Full, dry Riesling is its signature.

places.name: Forst an der Weinstrasse
places.note: The village whose growers carted black basalt from the Pechsteinkopf onto their sandstone vineyards, giving dense, smoky, long lived Riesling. Its named sites are the most famous in the Pfalz.

places.name: Kirchenstück
places.note: A small walled site beside the church that the 1828 survey placed at the very top of the Pfalz; the most complete and expensive Forst Riesling.

places.name: Jesuitengarten
places.note: The rounder, more perfumed neighbour of Kirchenstück, once the property of the Jesuits, as the name records.

places.name: Ungeheuer
places.note: The monster, a large and powerful site giving broad, spicy Riesling that needs time in bottle.

places.name: Pechstein
places.note: Named for the black basalt it sits on; the smokiest and most savoury Forst wine, with a flinty edge.

places.name: Deidesheim
places.note: A handsome small town with limestone and sandstone sites such as Hohenmorgen, Kalkofen, Grainhübel and Langenmorgen, home to several historic estates. Its Riesling is a shade more elegant and floral than Forst's.

places.name: Hohenmorgen
places.note: A compact limestone and sandstone site on the slope towards Forst, prized for fine, mineral, age-worthy Riesling.

places.name: Kalkofen
places.note: The lime kiln: limestone close to the surface gives taut, chalky Riesling that stands apart from the basalt wines next door.

places.name: Ruppertsberg
places.note: South of Deidesheim, with the Reiterpfad and the monopole Gaisböhl; gravelly, sandy sites giving earlier drinking, fruit forward Riesling.

places.name: Wachenheim
places.note: North of Forst, with Gerümpel, Rechbächel and Goldbächel; the home village of one of the region's great historic estates and a source of firm, slightly leaner Riesling.

places.name: Bad Dürkheim
places.note: The spa town at the centre of the Mittelhaardt, with the Michelsberg and Spielberg sites and the Wurstmarkt, the enormous September wine festival.

places.name: Kallstadt
places.note: A limestone village north of Bad Dürkheim whose Saumagen vineyard, sharing its name with the stuffed pig's stomach dish of the Pfalz, gives chalky, long lived dry Riesling.

places.name: Haardt, Gimmeldingen and Königsbach
places.note: Villages above Neustadt with the Bürgergarten, Mandelgarten and Idig sites; the southern Mittelhaardt, where Riesling meets Scheurebe, Rieslaner and Spätburgunder.

places.name: Neustadt an der Weinstrasse
places.note: The region's wine capital at the join of the two Bereiche, with the research institute at Mussbach.

places.name: Laumersheim and the Zellertal
places.note: The northern Pfalz towards Rheinhessen, on limestone and loess, where Spätburgunder and Riesling from Kirschgarten and the Schwarzer Herrgott have earned a modern reputation.

places.name: Südliche Weinstrasse
places.note: The southern Bereich from Neustadt to the French border, warmer and more varied in soil, long a source of bulk wine and now home to some of the region's finest estates. The Pinot family, Riesling on red slate and limestone, and Spätburgunder from Schweigen are the modern story.

places.name: Birkweiler
places.note: A village west of Landau whose Kastanienbusch, on red slate, gives among the most mineral dry Riesling in the Pfalz; the Mandelberg is its limestone neighbour.

places.name: Siebeldingen
places.note: Beside Birkweiler, with the Im Sonnenschein site of limestone and the vine breeding institute at Geilweilerhof, which bred Regent.

places.name: Schweigen
places.note: The last village before France, at the Deutsches Weintor; much of its Sonnenberg vineyard, with the Kammerberg and Sankt Paul parcels, lies in France, and the grapes are vinified in Germany as German wine.

places.name: Rhodt unter Rietburg
places.note: A village below the Rietburg ruin keeping ancient Traminer vines in its Rosengarten, a reminder that Gewürztraminer is an old Pfalz grape.

places.name: Landau in der Pfalz
places.note: The market town of the south, ringed by loess and loam vineyards that fill much of the region's everyday Dornfelder and Grauburgunder.

producers.name: Dr. Bürklin-Wolf
producers.why: The great biodynamic Mittelhaardt estate at Wachenheim, with the top Forst sites and a label hierarchy drawn from the 1828 Bavarian tax survey.

producers.name: Müller-Catoir
producers.why: The Haardt house that keeps Rieslaner and Scheurebe alive as serious wines, and the name to reach for when a question moves beyond Riesling.

producers.name: Reichsrat von Buhl
producers.why: A Deidesheim house and one of the three Bs of the Mittelhaardt with Bassermann-Jordan and Bürklin-Wolf, known for Forst Riesling GG and for traditional method Sekt.

producers.name: Bassermann-Jordan
producers.why: The Deidesheim estate with deep holdings in Forst and Deidesheim and one of the longest histories in the region.

producers.name: A. Christmann
producers.why: Gimmeldingen estate farming biodynamically, with the Königsbacher Idig as its flagship GG.

producers.name: Georg Mosbacher
producers.why: A Forst grower whose Ungeheuer, Pechstein and Kirchenstück show the village at the top of its game.

producers.name: Koehler-Ruprecht
producers.why: Kallstadt estate famous for long cask aged, dry Saumagen Riesling released years after the harvest.

producers.name: Ökonomierat Rebholz
producers.why: Siebeldingen pioneer of bone dry, unchaptalised Riesling and Spätburgunder from the Kastanienbusch and Im Sonnenschein.

producers.name: Dr. Wehrheim
producers.why: Birkweiler house whose Kastanienbusch Riesling and Weissburgunder put the red slate of the south on the map.

producers.name: Friedrich Becker
producers.why: Schweigen estate with Spätburgunder from the Kammerberg and Sankt Paul parcels of the Sonnenberg, which lie on the French side of the border.

producers.name: Knipser
producers.why: Laumersheim estate that led the northern Pfalz into serious Spätburgunder and dry Riesling.

exam: Place the Pfalz on the map: eastern foot of the Haardt, north of Alsace, south of Rheinhessen, warm and dry.
Know the two Bereiche, Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstrasse and Südliche Weinstrasse, and which is warmer.
Name the Mittelhaardt villages, Forst, Deidesheim, Ruppertsberg and Wachenheim, and the Forst crus Kirchenstück, Jesuitengarten, Ungeheuer and Pechstein.
Explain the basalt at Forst and the 1828 Bavarian tax survey as the roots of the Pfalz hierarchy.
Describe Pfalz Riesling against Mosel Riesling: riper, fuller, dry, spicy, higher alcohol.
Know the grapes beyond Riesling: Dornfelder, the Pinot family, Scheurebe, Rieslaner and Gewürztraminer.
Hold the German ladder, Prädikat by must weight, trocken and feinherb, VDP and the 2021 origin pyramid.
traps: Pfalz is not Palatinate wine of the sweet 1970s kind: today the region is dry first, and its Riesling is among Germany's fullest.
The Haardt is the hill range and Haardt is also a village above Neustadt; the shelter comes from the range.
Forst's basalt was quarried and spread by hand; it is not the bedrock of the whole village.
Mittelhaardt is a Bereich of the Pfalz, not a region of its own, and Südliche Weinstrasse is the other, not a wine road only.
Dornfelder is a 1955 Weinsberg crossing from Württemberg, though the Pfalz and Rheinhessen grow most of it.
Schweigen's best Spätburgunder parcels lie in France; the wine is still German Qualitätswein.
Grosses Gewächs since 2021 is also a legal term; the VDP's eagle marks only its members' wines.

cards.f: Pfalz: what shelters it and what does that do?
cards.b: The Haardt hills, the northern end of the Vosges, cast a rain shadow: the Pfalz is among Germany's driest, sunniest regions, warm enough for figs and almonds.

cards.f: The two Bereiche of the Pfalz, north and south
cards.b: Mittelhaardt-Deutsche Weinstrasse in the north (the classic Riesling villages); Südliche Weinstrasse in the south (warmer, Pinot family, Dornfelder).

cards.f: Four classic Mittelhaardt Riesling villages
cards.b: Forst, Deidesheim, Ruppertsberg and Wachenheim, with Bad Dürkheim and Kallstadt to the north.

cards.f: Forst's four famous single vineyards
cards.b: Kirchenstück, Jesuitengarten, Ungeheuer and Pechstein, all Grosse Lage sites; the 1828 survey placed Kirchenstück at the top of the Pfalz.

cards.f: What did Forst's growers do to their soil?
cards.b: They quarried black basalt from the Pechsteinkopf above the village and spread it over the sandstone vineyards to darken and warm the soil; Pechstein takes its name from it.

cards.f: Pfalz Riesling versus Mosel Riesling in one line
cards.b: Pfalz: riper, fuller, dry, spicy, higher alcohol, on sandstone, limestone and basalt. Mosel: lighter, lower alcohol, often off-dry, on slate.

cards.f: Which classification ranked Forster Kirchenstück top, and when?
cards.b: The Bavarian land tax survey of 1828, made while the Pfalz was Bavarian; one estate still prints P.C. and G.C. from it.

cards.f: Grapes the Pfalz grows beyond Riesling
cards.b: Dornfelder (the most planted red), Spätburgunder, Weissburgunder, Grauburgunder, Müller-Thurgau, Scheurebe, Rieslaner, Gewürztraminer.

cards.f: VDP Grosses Gewächs grapes allowed in the Pfalz
cards.b: Riesling, Weissburgunder and Spätburgunder.

cards.f: Schweigen: why is it a trap?
cards.b: Much of its Sonnenberg vineyard, with the Kammerberg and Sankt Paul parcels, lies over the border in France, yet the wine is vinified and sold as German wine.

questions.q: The Pfalz is one of the driest and warmest of Germany's thirteen regions. Which hill range shelters it from the west and makes that so?
questions.exp: The Haardt is the northern continuation of the Vosges and wrings the rain out of the westerlies. The Taunus shelters the Rheingau, the Odenwald backs the Hessische Bergstrasse and the Hunsrück lies between the Mosel and the Nahe.

questions.q: Which Bereich of the Pfalz holds the classic Riesling villages of Forst, Deidesheim and Wachenheim?
questions.exp: The Mittelhaardt is the northern Bereich and the historic heart of Pfalz Riesling. The Südliche Weinstrasse is the warmer southern Bereich, the Wonnegau is in Rheinhessen and the Ortenau is in Baden.

questions.q: Growers in one Mittelhaardt village spread crushed black volcanic rock over their vineyards to warm them. Name the village.
questions.exp: Basalt from the Pechsteinkopf above Forst was quarried and carted onto the sandstone below. The Pechstein vineyard takes its name from that stone, and Kirchenstück, Jesuitengarten and Ungeheuer are its neighbours.

questions.q: A Pfalz label reads Riesling Grosses Gewächs from a VDP member. What does the term tell a guest about the wine's sweetness?
questions.exp: Grosses Gewächs is the dry wine of a top classified site. The VDP keeps the Prädikat words Kabinett, Spätlese and Auslese for its wines that carry sweetness, so a GG is always trocken.

questions.q: Which grape is the most planted red variety of the Pfalz?
questions.exp: Dornfelder, bred at Weinsberg in 1955 for its deep colour, leads the red plantings of the Pfalz, which with Rheinhessen grows most of Germany's crop of it. Spätburgunder is the region's serious red, Portugieser its old everyday grape and Regent a disease resistant crossing from Geilweilerhof.

questions.q: The vineyards of the Pfalz were ranked for tax while the region belonged to another German state, and one estate still prints that ranking on its labels. In which year was that survey made?
questions.exp: The Bavarian land tax survey of 1828 placed Forster Kirchenstück at the top of the Pfalz. The Spätlese legend at Schloss Johannisberg dates from 1775, the Bordeaux classification from 1855 and the German wine law that created the Grosslagen from 1971.

questions.q: The last wine village of the Pfalz before France is known for Spätburgunder whose best sites lie across the border. Name the village.
questions.exp: Schweigen sits at the Deutsches Weintor at the southern end of the German Wine Road. Much of its Sonnenberg vineyard, with the Kammerberg parcel, is on French soil, and the grapes are brought back and vinified in Germany under German law.

questions.q: Which aromatic crossing of Silvaner and Riesling, with piercing acidity, do Pfalz estates keep for taut Auslese and sweeter wines?
questions.exp: Rieslaner was bred at Würzburg in 1921 and ripens late with high acid, which keeps its botrytis wines fresh. Scheurebe is Riesling crossed with Bukettraube, Kerner is Trollinger with Riesling, and Bacchus is a softer, early ripening crossing.

regions.name: Franken
regions.summary: Franken is Bavaria's wine region, strung along the river Main around Würzburg, far from the Rhine and the easternmost of the western group, looking towards Nuremberg rather than France. Its signature is dry Silvaner in the squat, flat Bocksbeutel flask, grown on shell limestone above Würzburg, on red sandstone to the west and on gypsum marl to the east. The climate is continental, with hard winters and a real spring frost risk, so early ripening grapes have always mattered more than Riesling. Würzburg's three great charitable and state estates carry centuries of history, and the Mainviereck in the west has become serious Spätburgunder country.

terroir.climate: Continental: cold winters, warm, often dry summers and a short growing season with a genuine risk of spring frost in the low ground and of early autumn cold. Rainfall is modest by German standards. The season favours grapes that ripen early and reliably, which is why Silvaner, Müller-Thurgau and Bacchus outweigh Riesling here, and why Riesling is kept for the warmest, steepest sites.
terroir.soils: Three rocks follow the river from west to east. The Mainviereck in the west sits on Buntsandstein, red sandstone, which suits Spätburgunder. The Maindreieck around Würzburg is Muschelkalk, shell limestone laid down in a shallow sea, giving taut, stony Silvaner. The Steigerwald to the east is Keuper, a gypsum bearing marl, giving broader, softer, earthier wines. Loess and loam fill the gentler ground.
terroir.topography: The Main meanders through a plateau and its bends throw up south facing slopes: the Stein above Würzburg, the great amphitheatre of the Escherndorfer Lump in the Volkach loop, the terraces at Klingenberg. Vineyards sit mostly between roughly 180 and 300 metres, higher and more exposed than the Rhine valleys, and the Steigerwald vines climb the escarpment that edges the region to the east.
terroir.water: The Main is the thread that holds Franken together. It flows west to join the Rhine at Mainz, and its bends, above all the Mainschleife at Volkach, give the river's reflected light and frost moderation to the slopes caught on their southern flanks. Away from the river the plateau is colder and the vine thins out.

grapes.name: Silvaner
grapes.styles: The region's identity: dry, earthy, herbal and pear scented, stony on Muschelkalk, broader on Keuper, and capable of fine botrytis sweet wines in the Lump.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Franken's volume grape for decades, giving soft, simple, early drinking dry whites from the gentler ground.

grapes.name: Bacchus
grapes.styles: An aromatic early ripening crossing and a Franken speciality, light, grapey and sometimes off-dry.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Kept for the best warm sites, where it gives firm, dry, mineral wine and occasional great sweet wines.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder on the red sandstone of the Mainviereck at Bürgstadt and Klingenberg is among Germany's finest, fragrant and firm.

grapes.name: Scheurebe
grapes.styles: Grapefruit and blackcurrant leaf aromatics, made dry or as sweet Auslese by the Würzburg estates.

grapes.name: Rieslaner
grapes.styles: Bred at Würzburg in 1921 from Silvaner and Riesling; late, acid and rare, it makes razor edged Beerenauslese.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder gives creamy dry whites and is gaining ground beside Silvaner on the limestone.

grapes.name: Domina
grapes.styles: A deeply coloured Portugieser and Spätburgunder crossing planted for sturdy, rustic Franken reds.

wines.note: Dry, savoury, with pear, hay and a stony, almost salty finish, moderate alcohol and gentle acidity. Serve it with asparagus, river fish, pork and the Franconian table it was made for.
The dry single site top wine of the Würzburger Stein, the Escherndorfer Lump or the Iphofen slopes: fuller, longer and age-worthy, often lees aged in old oak.
Soft, light and floral, the everyday Franken white, happiest young and cold with a Bratwurst.
Firm, dry and mineral from the warmest sites, leaner than the Pfalz and more austere than the Rheingau.
Light, aromatic and grapey, often with a little sweetness; a Franken speciality that reads like a gentle Muscat.
Pinot Noir from red sandstone at Bürgstadt and Klingenberg: fragrant red cherry, fine tannin and real length, among Germany's best.

wines.style: Silvaner and Riesling Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese
wines.note: Botrytis wines from the Lump and the Stein, rare because the dry autumn seldom allows them, with Silvaner's earth and Riesling's acid keeping them bright.

made.viticulture: Franken grows at the climatic limit for a German region without the Rhine's help, so the first decision is the grape. Silvaner ripens a week or two ahead of Riesling and sets reliably after a cold spring, which is why it became the region's identity, and Müller-Thurgau and Bacchus follow the same logic. Spring frost is the great hazard; the river slopes escape it and the plateau does not, and growers light fires or run wind machines in a bad April. The steep sites, the Stein and the Innere Leiste above Würzburg, the Lump at Escherndorf and the Klingenberg terraces with their dry stone walls, are worked largely by hand, while the Keuper hills of the Steigerwald and the loess ground are mechanised. Harvest runs from September for Müller-Thurgau and Bacchus into October for Silvaner and Riesling, and the dry autumns that make botrytis rare are also what keep the fruit clean. Silvaner was first planted in Germany at Castell in 1659, and the grape has never left.
made.winemaking: Franken finishes its wine dry almost without exception, and has done so for far longer than the rest of Germany; sweetness is the exception kept for Auslese and above. Silvaner and Riesling are fermented in stainless steel or in the large old oak casks of the Würzburg cellars, where the great estates' vaults run for hundreds of metres under the Residenz and the Juliusspital, and the top Grosses Gewächs bottlings rest on their lees in wood through the winter. Malolactic conversion is avoided for the whites to keep the fruit fresh. The Mainviereck's Spätburgunder is made in the Burgundian manner with barriques and some whole bunches. The wine then goes into the Bocksbeutel, the flattened flask protected for Franken under European law, which a guest recognises across a room and which will not lie down in a wine rack. Sweet wines appear only when the autumn allows.

law.classification: Franken is one of the thirteen Anbaugebiete, so a Franken Qualitätswein or Prädikatswein must name the region on its label and carry the official test number. German law ranks by must weight at harvest, Qualitätswein and then the Prädikat ladder from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese, and the 2021 reform added the origin pyramid of Anbaugebiet, Region, Ort and Einzellage, with Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs as protected terms for dry single site wines, binding in full from the 2026 vintage. Franken has three Bereiche, Mainviereck and Maindreieck named for the river's shape and Steigerwald for the hills, and they match its three rocks. The Bocksbeutel is protected for Franken and for two pockets of neighbouring Baden, Tauberfranken and the Neuweier vineyards. Within the VDP's private pyramid, Franken's Grosses Gewächs admits Silvaner alongside Riesling and the Burgunder family, the clearest case of a regional variety written into the top tier.
tiers: Wine without geographical indication, the floor.
The protected geographical indication level; Franken's Landwein carries the Bavarian name Landwein Main.
Quality wine from Franken alone, with a test number; the must may be enriched within the zone A limit.
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese by must weight at picking, never enriched; in Franken most Kabinett and Spätlese are fermented dry.

Protected terms for dry wine of protected origin from a named single vineyard: the ordinance caps Erstes Gewächs at 60 hectolitres per hectare, 70 on steep slopes, and holds Grosses Gewächs to a lower cap, hand picking and a later release.
The association's top site class; a dry Franken GG may be Silvaner as well as Riesling or a Burgunder.
labels: The flattened, round bellied flask protected for Franken and two pockets of Baden.
The three Bereiche: the square of the Main in the west, the triangle around Würzburg, the escarpment in the east.
Legally dry, at most 4 grams per litre of sugar or up to 9 where acidity is within 2 grams of it; Franken's default style.
The old trade name for the wine of the Würzburger Stein, once used loosely for all Franken wine.
The dry wine of a top classified site; Silvaner qualifies in Franken.
Franconian wine, the regional name on cooperative and generic bottlings.
Estate bottled from the estate's own grapes.

places.name: Maindreieck
places.note: The central Bereich, the triangle the Main draws around Würzburg, on Muschelkalk shell limestone. It holds the region's capital, its three historic estates and its most famous sites, and gives the tautest, stoniest Silvaner.

places.name: Würzburg
places.note: The baroque capital of Franken, whose Stein vineyard rises directly above the city on limestone. The Juliusspital, the Bürgerspital and the Staatlicher Hofkeller under the Residenz all have their cellars here.

places.name: Würzburger Stein
places.note: The great south facing limestone slope above the city, the origin of the word Steinwein; dry Silvaner and Riesling of stone and herbs, and historic sweet wines.

places.name: Innere Leiste
places.note: A steep, warm site beneath the Marienberg fortress, across the river from the Stein, favoured for Riesling and Silvaner.

places.name: Randersacker
places.note: A limestone village just upstream of Würzburg with the Pfülben and Sonnenstuhl sites, a classic source of firm dry Silvaner.

places.name: Escherndorf
places.note: A village on the Mainschleife, the great loop of the river near Volkach, whose Lump is a steep limestone amphitheatre giving the region's richest Silvaner and its rare botrytis wines.

places.name: Volkach
places.note: The market town on the Mainschleife loop, the centre of the Mainschleife's vineyards and of the region's wine tourism.

places.name: Steigerwald
places.note: The eastern Bereich on Keuper, gypsum bearing marl, where the vineyards climb the Steigerwald escarpment. Its Silvaner is broader, softer and more earthy than Würzburg's, and it holds the first recorded German Silvaner.

places.name: Iphofen
places.note: A walled town with the Julius-Echter-Berg and Kronsberg on gypsum marl; Iphofen Silvaner and Riesling are powerful and spicy.

places.name: Castell
places.note: The village of the counts of Castell whose Schlossberg saw Germany's first documented Silvaner planting in 1659.

places.name: Rödelsee
places.note: Beside Iphofen, with the Küchenmeister site; a smaller source of fine Keuper Silvaner.

places.name: Mainviereck
places.note: The western Bereich, the square of the Main towards Aschaffenburg, on Buntsandstein red sandstone. It is Franken's red wine corner, and the Spätburgunder of Bürgstadt and Klingenberg stands with the Ahr's and Baden's best.

places.name: Bürgstadt
places.note: The Centgrafenberg on red sandstone is the Mainviereck's great Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder site.

places.name: Klingenberg
places.note: Narrow dry stone terraces of red sandstone above the Main, the Schlossberg among them, worked by hand for Spätburgunder.

producers.name: Horst Sauer
producers.why: The Escherndorf estate whose Lump Silvaner is the benchmark for dry Franken and whose botrytis wines are among Germany's purest.

producers.name: Juliusspital
producers.why: The Würzburg charitable foundation of 1576, one of Germany's largest estates, with Stein, Lump and Julius-Echter-Berg holdings funding its hospital.

producers.name: Bürgerspital zum Heiligen Geist
producers.why: The older Würzburg charity, founded in 1316, with prime Stein parcels and a historic Steinwein cellar.

producers.name: Staatlicher Hofkeller Würzburg
producers.why: The Bavarian state estate in the vaults beneath the Residenz, heir to the prince-bishops' cellar.

producers.name: Rudolf Fürst
producers.why: The Bürgstadt estate that proved red sandstone Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder could rank with Germany's finest.

producers.name: Hans Wirsching
producers.why: The leading Iphofen house for spicy Keuper Silvaner and Riesling from the Julius-Echter-Berg.

producers.name: Fürstlich Castell'sches Domänenamt
producers.why: The princely Castell estate that keeps the 1659 Silvaner story and makes textbook Steigerwald wine.

producers.name: Weingut am Stein
producers.why: A Würzburg estate on the Stein itself, farming organically and known for modern, precise Silvaner.

producers.name: Zehnthof Luckert
producers.why: Sulzfeld growers of old vine Silvaner from Muschelkalk with a cult following.

exam: Place Franken: Bavaria, on the Main around Würzburg, the region furthest east of the western group.
Say the signature in one breath: dry Silvaner in the Bocksbeutel on Muschelkalk.
Know the three Bereiche and their three rocks: Mainviereck and sandstone, Maindreieck and shell limestone, Steigerwald and gypsum marl.
Name the Würzburger Stein, the Escherndorfer Lump and Iphofen's Julius-Echter-Berg, and which rock each sits on.
Know the three historic Würzburg estates and the 1659 Silvaner planting at Castell.
Remember Franken is continental with spring frost, so early ripeners outnumber Riesling.
Know that the Mainviereck is Spätburgunder country on red sandstone.
traps: Silvaner here is dry and savoury; it is the same grape as Alsace's Sylvaner but not the same wine.
The Bocksbeutel is protected for Franken and two pockets of Baden, not for Germany at large.
Franken's river is the Main, not the Rhine, and its capital is Würzburg, not Nuremberg.
Escherndorfer Lump is a single Einzellage despite its unflattering name, not a Grosslage.
Müller-Thurgau is Riesling crossed with Madeleine Royale, not with Silvaner, however Franconian it feels.
Rieslaner was bred at Würzburg from Silvaner and Riesling; Scheurebe is Riesling and Bukettraube.
Franken is in Bavaria, but the Bayerischer Bodensee vineyards belong to Württemberg's region, not Franken's.

cards.f: Franken in one line: grape, bottle, rock
cards.b: Dry Silvaner, in the Bocksbeutel, on Muschelkalk shell limestone around Würzburg on the river Main.

cards.f: The three Bereiche of Franken and their rocks
cards.b: Mainviereck (west): Buntsandstein red sandstone. Maindreieck (centre, Würzburg): Muschelkalk shell limestone. Steigerwald (east): Keuper gypsum marl.

cards.f: Place Franken: its river, its state and its capital
cards.b: The Main; Bavaria; Würzburg. The Main flows west to join the Rhine at Mainz.

cards.f: Where and when was Silvaner first planted in Germany?
cards.b: At Castell in the Steigerwald, in 1659.

cards.f: The three historic Würzburg estates
cards.b: Bürgerspital zum Heiligen Geist (1316), Juliusspital (1576), Staatlicher Hofkeller (the state cellar under the Residenz).

cards.f: Franken's famous sites: name three and their villages
cards.b: Würzburger Stein (Würzburg), Escherndorfer Lump (Escherndorf, on the Mainschleife), Julius-Echter-Berg (Iphofen).

cards.f: Why does Franken grow Silvaner rather than Riesling?
cards.b: A continental climate with spring frost and a short season: Silvaner ripens a week or two earlier and sets reliably. Riesling is kept for the warmest sites.

cards.f: Where else may the Bocksbeutel be used?
cards.b: Two pockets of Baden: Tauberfranken in the north and the Neuweier vineyards near Baden-Baden.

cards.f: Franken's red wine corner
cards.b: The Mainviereck on red sandstone: Bürgstadt (Centgrafenberg) and Klingenberg's terraces, for Spätburgunder and Frühburgunder.

questions.q: Which grape is Franken's signature, finished dry and showing an earthy, herbal, pear scented character?
questions.exp: Silvaner ripens earlier than Riesling and takes its stony character from the Muschelkalk around Würzburg. Müller-Thurgau and Bacchus are grown for volume and aroma, and Riesling is kept for the warmest sites.

questions.q: A squat, round bellied flask marks the wine of Franken and is protected for it under European law. What is the bottle called?
questions.exp: The Bocksbeutel is reserved for Franken and for two small pockets of Baden, Tauberfranken and the Neuweier area. It is instantly recognisable and will not lie flat in a rack.

questions.q: Which Bereich of Franken sits on Keuper, the gypsum bearing marl, around Iphofen and Castell?
questions.exp: The Steigerwald is the eastern Bereich on Keuper and gives broader, softer Silvaner. The Mainviereck is red sandstone, the Maindreieck is shell limestone, and Tauberfranken is a Bereich of Baden.

questions.q: Germany's first documented planting of Silvaner was made in 1659 in a Steigerwald village. Name the village.
questions.exp: The counts of Castell recorded the planting on their Schlossberg in 1659, and the estate still makes Silvaner from it. The date is the anchor for every question on the grape's German history.

questions.q: Along which river do Franken's vineyards lie?
questions.exp: The Main runs through Würzburg and west to the Rhine at Mainz, and its bends make the region's south facing sites. The Neckar is Württemberg's river, the Nahe has its own region, and the Tauber is a small tributary shared with Baden.

questions.q: Which Würzburg estate was founded in 1576 by a prince-bishop as a charitable hospital that wine still funds?
questions.exp: Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn founded the Juliusspital in 1576. The Bürgerspital is older, from 1316, the Hofkeller is the Bavarian state's cellar under the Residenz, and Kloster Eberbach is a Rheingau monastery.

questions.q: A steep limestone amphitheatre above a loop of the Main at Escherndorf gives Franken's richest Silvaner and its rare botrytis wines. What is the vineyard called?
questions.exp: The Escherndorfer Lump sits on the Mainschleife near Volkach, and despite its unflattering name it is a single Einzellage. The leading Escherndorf estate built its reputation on it.

questions.q: Which Bereich of Franken grows serious Spätburgunder on red Buntsandstein at Bürgstadt and Klingenberg?
questions.exp: The Mainviereck is the western square of the Main where red sandstone surfaces, and its Pinot Noir ranks with the Ahr's and Baden's. The Maindreieck is limestone, the Steigerwald is marl, and the Kraichgau is in Baden.

regions.name: Württemberg
regions.summary: Württemberg is the vineyard of the Neckar and its tributaries around Stuttgart and Heilbronn, and it is Germany's red wine region: unusually, more of it is planted to red grapes than white. Trollinger, the pale, light red the Alto Adige calls Schiava, fills the local quarter litre glass, Lemberger, which Austria calls Blaufränkisch, is the serious red, and Schwarzriesling, Spätburgunder and Dornfelder follow. Riesling leads the whites. Keuper marl and Muschelkalk on terraced valley slopes, a sheltered continental climate, powerful cooperatives and a population that drinks nearly everything it makes are the rest of the story, with the Weinsberg school breeding the region's crossings since 1868.

terroir.climate: Continental, with cold winters, warm summers and a growing season sheltered by the Swabian hills from the worst of the west. The Neckar valley and its side valleys trap warmth, which is what lets late ripening Trollinger and Lemberger succeed this far north, while low ground near the rivers suffers spring and autumn frost. Rainfall is moderate and the summers can be dry.
terroir.soils: Keuper dominates: gypsum bearing marls and coloured clays of the Triassic that give the Remstal, the Stuttgart slopes and the Heilbronn country their sturdy reds. Muschelkalk shell limestone surfaces along the middle Neckar at Besigheim, Hessigheim and Mundelsheim and in the Tauber country to the north. Loess and loam cover the gentler ground, and the Bodensee vineyards sit on glacial moraine.
terroir.topography: The Neckar cuts a winding valley with steep south facing flanks that were terraced centuries ago behind dry stone walls, the Steillagen that are the region's pride and its labour problem. Away from the river the vineyards spread over rolling Keuper hills between orchards and towns, often inside the suburbs of Stuttgart itself. Two small outposts sit far to the south on the shores of Lake Constance.
terroir.water: The Neckar is the spine, joined by the Rems, the Enz, the Kocher and the Jagst, with the Tauber marking the north. The river's bends make the terraced sites and moderate the frost on their slopes. Lake Constance, the Bodensee, moderates the two detached southern Bereiche and gives them light and a long autumn.

grapes.name: Trollinger
grapes.styles: The region's everyday red, pale, light, soft and often a touch sweet, drunk young and cool by the quarter litre; Schiava or Vernatsch in the Alto Adige.

grapes.name: Lemberger
grapes.styles: Blaufränkisch under its Württemberg name: the serious red, dark fruited, peppery and firm, dry and increasingly barrel aged, and admitted to the VDP's Grosses Gewächs here.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: The main white, dry and firm from the Neckar terraces and the Remstal, with more body than the Mosel's.

grapes.name: Schwarzriesling
grapes.styles: Pinot Meunier, called black Riesling though it is no Riesling; a soft, pale red speciality.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder from the best Keuper and limestone slopes is the modern ambition alongside Lemberger.

grapes.name: Samtrot
grapes.styles: A velvety red mutation of Schwarzriesling selected at Weinsberg, a Württemberg curiosity.

grapes.name: Dornfelder
grapes.styles: Bred at Weinsberg in 1955 for colour; deep, soft reds for the everyday table.

grapes.name: Kerner
grapes.styles: The 1929 Weinsberg crossing of Trollinger and Riesling, a reliable aromatic white.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Simple, soft dry whites from the easier ground, often sold as Rivaner.

wines.note: Pale ruby, light bodied, with strawberry and a soft, often slightly sweet finish; serve it cool in a Viertele, the local quarter litre, with Maultaschen or a sausage salad.
The classic local blend, Trollinger's lightness given a little colour and grip by Lemberger; easy, cheerful and made for the Besen, the seasonal grower's tavern.
Dark cherry, black pepper, firm tannin and bright acidity, from unoaked village wine to barrique aged single site GG; Württemberg's answer to a serious red, good with game and roast beef.
A Rotling: red and white grapes fermented together, pale, fresh and local, protected to Württemberg at Qualitätswein level and above.
Dry, firm and fuller than the Mosel's, from Keuper and limestone terraces; the white that accompanies the region's reds at table.
Pinot Meunier as a still red: pale, soft, red fruited and gentle, rarely seen outside the region.
Pinot Noir from the best slopes, fragrant and structured in the modern style, increasingly a Grosses Gewächs grape here.

made.viticulture: Württemberg's vines are planted mostly in red grapes, which only the tiny Ahr otherwise matches, and they are tended by thousands of small growers who deliver to cooperatives; the cooperative share of the crop is among the largest in the country. The old terraces along the Neckar, Hessigheim's Felsengärten and the walls at Besigheim and Mundelsheim among them, are narrow, steep and hand worked, and keeping them alive is the region's running struggle; the Keuper hills are mechanised. Trollinger ripens very late and needs the warmest ground, which is why it was planted where Lemberger and Spätburgunder would now do better, and high yields long kept it pale and simple. Frost on low ground and hail are the hazards. The state school at Weinsberg, founded in 1868, bred Kerner in 1929 and Dornfelder in 1955 and selected Samtrot, so the region's grape list carries its own research history. Harvest runs from late September into November for the latest Trollinger.
made.winemaking: Most Württemberg wine is made by cooperatives at scale and drunk within the region, so the traditional style is light: Trollinger sees a short maceration, little or no oak and often a touch of residual sugar, and is bottled young. Schillerwein is made by fermenting red and white grapes together, a Rotling, and Weissherbst by pressing a single red variety as rosé. The serious work is in Lemberger and Spätburgunder, where a generation of estates picks lower yields, ferments with longer maceration and ages in barrique, producing Grosses Gewächs reds that the rest of Germany now takes seriously. Riesling is fermented dry, usually in stainless steel. Sekt by the traditional method is a growing side line, and the Besen, the grower's seasonal tavern marked by a broom over the door, remains the natural place to taste the region's wine with its food.

law.classification: Württemberg is one of the thirteen Anbaugebiete, so its Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein carry the region's name and an official test number, ranked by must weight at harvest from Qualitätswein through the Prädikat ladder, with the 2021 reform's origin pyramid of Anbaugebiet, Region, Ort and Einzellage laid over it and Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs as protected dry single site terms, binding in full from the 2026 vintage. The region has six Bereiche: Remstal-Stuttgart, Württembergisch Unterland, Kocher-Jagst-Tauber, Oberer Neckar, Württembergischer Bodensee and, across the state line, Bayerischer Bodensee. Schillerwein is a Rotling protected to Württemberg at Qualitätswein level or above. Within the VDP's private pyramid the region's Grosses Gewächs admits Lemberger alongside Riesling and Spätburgunder, so the Blaufränkisch synonym appears on top tier German labels.
tiers: The protected geographical indication level, here Schwäbischer Landwein.
Quality wine from Württemberg alone, test number required, enrichment allowed within zone A.
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese by must weight at picking; a Trollinger Kabinett is a common sight and is often lightly sweet.

Protected terms for dry wine of protected origin from a named single vineyard: the ordinance caps Erstes Gewächs at 60 hectolitres per hectare, 70 on steep slopes, and holds Grosses Gewächs to a lower cap, hand picking and a later release.
The association's top site class; Lemberger, Riesling and Spätburgunder are the grapes seen as GG here.
labels: A Württemberg Rotling: red and white grapes fermented together, Qualitätswein or above.
A rosé from one named red variety, Qualitätswein or above.
The regional name for Blaufränkisch; Limberger is a permitted spelling.
The regional name for the grape the Alto Adige calls Schiava or Vernatsch.
The quarter litre glass in which the region drinks its Trollinger.
A grower's seasonal tavern, marked by a broom over the door, allowed to open and sell its own wine for a limited number of weeks each year.
Legally dry, at most 4 grams per litre of sugar or up to 9 where acidity is within 2 grams of it.

places.name: Remstal-Stuttgart
places.note: The Bereich around the state capital and the Rems valley to its east, on Keuper marl. Stuttgart has vineyards inside its city limits, and Fellbach, Untertürkheim and the Remstal villages hold several of the region's leading estates for Lemberger, Riesling and Spätburgunder.

places.name: Fellbach
places.note: A town at the edge of Stuttgart whose Lämmler site on Keuper is a reference for Lemberger and Riesling Grosses Gewächs.

places.name: Untertürkheim and Stuttgart
places.note: Steep Keuper slopes above the Neckar within the city, with the Mönchberg and Herzogenberg sites among them.

places.name: Remstal
places.note: The Rems valley east of Stuttgart, with Stetten's Pulvermächer and other Keuper sites giving some of the region's finest Riesling.

places.name: Württembergisch Unterland
places.note: The largest Bereich, the lower land around Heilbronn and the middle Neckar, on Keuper and Muschelkalk. It holds the terraced river sites, the great cooperatives and the villages that make most of the region's Trollinger and Lemberger.

places.name: Heilbronn
places.note: The wine town of the north with large cooperative cellars and the Wartberg vineyard above it; Neckar terraces run south from here.

places.name: Besigheim, Hessigheim and Mundelsheim
places.note: The middle Neckar's terraced Muschelkalk sites behind dry stone walls, the Hessigheimer Felsengärten the most dramatic, worked by hand for Trollinger, Lemberger and Riesling.

places.name: Weinsberg
places.note: Home of the state viticultural school founded in 1868, the oldest in Germany, which bred Kerner and Dornfelder and keeps its own estate on the Schemelsberg.

places.name: Schwaigern and Bönnigheim
places.note: Keuper villages of the Heilbronn and Zabergäu country whose estates built Lemberger's modern reputation.

places.name: Brackenheim
places.note: The Zabergäu town often called Germany's largest red wine commune, on Keuper, with Trollinger and Lemberger throughout.

places.name: Kocher-Jagst-Tauber
places.note: The small northern Bereich on Muschelkalk along three rivers, cooler, with more white grapes than the rest of the region, and close in style to neighbouring Tauberfranken.

places.name: Oberer Neckar
places.note: A tiny Bereich of scattered vineyards up the Neckar around Rottenburg and Tübingen, mostly for local consumption.

places.name: Württembergischer Bodensee and Bayerischer Bodensee
places.note: Two detached Bereiche on the shores of Lake Constance; the Bavarian one, around Lindau, lies in Bavaria yet belongs to the Württemberg region, with Müller-Thurgau and Spätburgunder on moraine.

producers.name: Aldinger
producers.why: The Fellbach estate whose Lämmler Lemberger and Riesling GG set the standard for modern Württemberg.

producers.name: Schnaitmann
producers.why: Fellbach grower who made the case for serious Spätburgunder and Lemberger from Keuper.

producers.name: Graf Neipperg
producers.why: The Schwaigern house most associated with Lemberger, which it has championed for generations.

producers.name: Dautel
producers.why: Bönnigheim estate known for barrel aged Lemberger and Spätburgunder of real polish.

producers.name: Graf Adelmann
producers.why: The Kleinbottwar estate at Burg Schaubeck, a long standing name for Lemberger and Samtrot.

producers.name: Wöhrwag
producers.why: Untertürkheim estate working steep Stuttgart slopes for Riesling and Lemberger.

producers.name: Herzog von Württemberg
producers.why: The ducal estate at Ludwigsburg, a historic name with holdings across the region.

producers.name: Karl Haidle
producers.why: Remstal estate whose Stetten Pulvermächer Riesling shows the valley's white side.

producers.name: Staatsweingut Weinsberg
producers.why: The state school's own estate, where the region's crossings were bred and are still shown.

exam: Place Württemberg: the Neckar and its tributaries around Stuttgart and Heilbronn, south east of the Rhine regions.
Say the signature: Germany's red wine region, more red than white, Trollinger for everyday and Lemberger for serious.
Decode the synonyms: Trollinger is Schiava, Lemberger is Blaufränkisch, Schwarzriesling is Pinot Meunier.
Know Schillerwein as a Rotling, red and white grapes fermented together, protected to Württemberg.
Know Weinsberg, founded 1868, as the school that bred Kerner (1929) and Dornfelder (1955).
Name the six Bereiche and remember the Bayerischer Bodensee sits in Bavaria yet belongs to this region.
Know Keuper marl and Muschelkalk terraces as the soils, and the cooperatives as the makers.
traps: Schwarzriesling is Pinot Meunier and has nothing to do with Riesling.
Trollinger is Schiava, not a Pinot and not a crossing; it needs the warmest ground because it ripens so late.
Schillerwein is not a blend of finished wines and not a rosé from one grape; it is a Rotling, co-fermented.
Weissherbst is the single variety rosé; do not confuse it with Schillerwein.
Dornfelder is a Weinsberg crossing from Württemberg, though the Pfalz and Rheinhessen grow most of it.
Württemberg's Riesling is dry and fuller than the Mosel's; do not read the region as sweet.
The Bayerischer Bodensee is in Bavaria but is a Bereich of Württemberg, not of Franken.

cards.f: Württemberg in one line
cards.b: The Neckar region around Stuttgart and Heilbronn, Germany's red wine region: Trollinger for everyday, Lemberger for serious, Riesling the white, cooperatives the makers.

cards.f: Three Württemberg synonyms a server must decode
cards.b: Trollinger = Schiava (Vernatsch). Lemberger = Blaufränkisch. Schwarzriesling = Pinot Meunier (Müllerrebe).

cards.f: What is Schillerwein?
cards.b: A Württemberg Rotling: red and white grapes fermented together, pale and fresh, Qualitätswein or above. Not a blend of finished wines and not Weissherbst.

cards.f: What is Weissherbst?
cards.b: A rosé made from a single named red variety at Qualitätswein level or above, common in Baden and Württemberg.

cards.f: The Weinsberg school: when, and which grapes?
cards.b: Founded 1868, Germany's oldest viticultural school. Bred Kerner (Trollinger x Riesling, 1929) and Dornfelder (1955), selected Samtrot.

cards.f: The six Bereiche of Württemberg
cards.b: Remstal-Stuttgart, Württembergisch Unterland (largest), Kocher-Jagst-Tauber, Oberer Neckar, Württembergischer Bodensee, Bayerischer Bodensee.

cards.f: Württemberg's two soils and where each shows
cards.b: Keuper gypsum marl under the Remstal, Stuttgart and Heilbronn slopes; Muschelkalk shell limestone on the terraced middle Neckar at Besigheim, Hessigheim and Mundelsheim.

cards.f: Which red grapes may be VDP Grosses Gewächs in Württemberg?
cards.b: Lemberger and Spätburgunder, alongside Riesling for the whites.

questions.q: Along which river and its tributaries do Württemberg's vineyards lie?
questions.exp: The Neckar winds past Stuttgart and Heilbronn, joined by the Rems, Enz, Kocher and Jagst. The Main is Franken's river, the Rhine is Baden's western edge, and the Danube crosses the south of the state without a wine region on its banks.

questions.q: Württemberg's pale, light everyday red is the grape the Alto Adige calls Schiava. What does the German label say?
questions.exp: Trollinger ripens very late and gives a soft, strawberry scented red drunk young and cool by the quarter litre. The name is a worn down form of Tirolinger, from the Tyrol.

questions.q: Lemberger, the serious red of Württemberg, is the same grape as which Austrian variety?
questions.exp: Lemberger and Blaufränkisch are one grape, Kékfrankos in Hungary. Zweigelt is a crossing of Blaufränkisch and Sankt Laurent, and Portugieser is an older, paler red.

questions.q: A Württemberg Schillerwein arrives pale pink at the table. How was it made?
opts: A rosé pressed from Trollinger alone
Red and white grapes fermented together
A blend of finished red and white wines
A red wine bottled with a light sparkle
questions.exp: Schillerwein is a Rotling, which by law means red and white grapes or their must fermented together. A single variety rosé is a Weissherbst, and blending finished red and white wine is not permitted for a quality wine.

questions.q: Which Württemberg town holds the state viticultural school, founded in 1868, where Kerner and Dornfelder were bred?
questions.exp: Weinsberg near Heilbronn is Germany's oldest viticultural school and keeps its own estate. Kerner came from it in 1929 and Dornfelder in 1955.

questions.q: Schwarzriesling is a speciality red of Württemberg. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Schwarzriesling, also called Müllerrebe, is Meunier, the Champagne grape, and its name has nothing to do with Riesling. Frühburgunder is the early ripening mutation of Pinot Noir, and Samtrot is a velvety mutation of Schwarzriesling selected at Weinsberg.

questions.q: Which Bereich of Württemberg holds the vineyards inside the state capital and the Rems valley to its east?
questions.exp: Remstal-Stuttgart takes in the city slopes, Fellbach and the Rems villages. The Unterland is the larger Heilbronn country to the north, Kocher-Jagst-Tauber is the cool northern fringe and the Oberer Neckar is a tiny upstream outpost.

regions.name: Baden
regions.summary: Baden is Germany's southernmost and warmest region, a long, broken strip that runs from Lake Constance up the Rhine past Freiburg, the Kaiserstuhl and the Ortenau to Heidelberg, with an outpost on the Tauber in the north, facing Alsace across the river for most of its length. It alone of the thirteen sits in the warmer European wine zone B. It belongs to the Pinot family: Spätburgunder above all, then Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder, with Müller-Thurgau for volume, Riesling in the Ortenau and Gutedel in the Markgräflerland. The Kaiserstuhl, an extinct volcano capped with loess terraces, is its hottest and most famous corner, and cooperatives make most of its wine.

terroir.climate: The warmest of the German regions. The Upper Rhine plain lies between the Vosges, which take the rain, and the Black Forest, which shelters the east, and the Burgundian Gate to the south west lets Mediterranean warmth up the valley. Summers are hot and sunny, winters mild, and the Kaiserstuhl records the highest temperatures in German viticulture. The Bodensee vineyards are cooler and higher, and the Tauber outpost in the north is continental.
terroir.soils: Deep wind blown loess covers much of the plain and the Kaiserstuhl's terraces, holding water and warmth. Beneath it the Kaiserstuhl is volcanic rock, which gives its most mineral Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder. The Ortenau's foothills are granite and gneiss, suited to Riesling. The Breisgau at Malterdingen and much of the Markgräflerland sit on limestone and marl, Tauberfranken on Muschelkalk, and the Bodensee vines on glacial moraine.
terroir.topography: For most of its length the vineyards sit on the western foothills of the Black Forest, facing the Rhine, with the Kaiserstuhl and the smaller Tuniberg standing as isolated hills out in the plain. The Kaiserstuhl's slopes were recut into enormous terraces in the 1960s and 1970s. The Bodensee vineyards above Meersburg are among the highest in Germany, above 400 metres, and the Kraichgau and Bergstrasse to the north are gentle loess hills.
terroir.water: The Rhine forms the western edge and the border with France and Switzerland, and its wide plain stores the summer heat. Lake Constance, the Bodensee, is Germany's largest lake and gives the southern outpost its reflected light and a long, mild autumn. The Tauber in the far north links the region to Franken.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Spätburgunder is Baden's grape and the reason Germany is the world's third largest Pinot Noir producer: from pale, soft village wine to Burgundian, barrique aged Grosses Gewächs on volcanic rock and limestone.

grapes.name: Pinot Gris / Grigio
grapes.styles: Grauburgunder, dry, pear and nut scented and full; the Kaiserstuhl's signature white, with Ruländer the older name for the richer, sweeter style.

grapes.name: Müller-Thurgau
grapes.styles: Baden's volume white, soft and simple, from the loess of the plain and the Bodensee.

grapes.name: Pinot Blanc
grapes.styles: Weissburgunder gives creamy, understated dry whites that suit oak and are admitted to Grosses Gewächs here.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: A speciality of the Ortenau, where Durbach calls it Klingelberger and grows it on granite, firm and dry.

grapes.name: Gutedel
grapes.styles: Chasselas, brought to the Markgräflerland in 1780; soft, light, low acid wine drunk young and locally.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Planted on Baden's limestone with Burgundian intent and taken as seriously as the Pinot whites by the leading estates.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Traminer, called Clevner in the Ortenau around Durbach, dry and spicy.

wines.note: Pinot Noir from volcanic rock and loess: ripe cherry, smoke and spice with real body, the fullest German Pinot. Serve it just below room temperature with duck, lamb or a mushroom dish.
The dry single site top wine, often from Burgundian clones with whole bunches and barrique, built to age; the Kaiserstuhl, the Breisgau and the Ortenau all produce them.
Dry Pinot Gris of pear, almond and weight, often lees aged and sometimes oaked; the white a Baden table opens with, good with spargel and river fish.
Dry Pinot Blanc, creamy and gentle, the region's quiet food wine.
Light, soft, low in acid and alcohol, drunk young and cold in the Markgräflerland with a plate of ham; the German face of Chasselas.
Dry, firm Riesling from granite at Durbach and Neuweier, the latter sold in the Bocksbeutel.
A rosé pressed from Spätburgunder alone, pale and dry, a Baden and Bodensee tradition.
Baden's protected Rotling, Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder fermented together, pale copper and refreshing.

made.viticulture: Baden's warmth changes the grower's questions. Ripeness is rarely in doubt, so the work is in restraint: moderating vigour on deep loess, shading fruit against sunburn, and holding yields down so that Spätburgunder has colour and tannin rather than the pale, washed out wines of the past. The Kaiserstuhl's loess slopes were recut into huge stepped terraces by the land consolidation of the 1960s and 1970s, which made them workable by machine but changed their face for good, and some growers have since returned to the small old terraces. Burgundian clones of Pinot Noir replaced the high yielding German selections from the 1980s, and organic farming is widespread. Harvest comes earlier than in the north, often from early September, and drought and hail are the hazards rather than frost or rot. Most growers deliver to cooperatives, which make the bulk of Baden's wine, and the European zone B rules that cap enrichment lower here are a formal admission that the sun does the job.
made.winemaking: Baden's cellars follow Burgundy more closely than any in Germany. Spätburgunder is made with cold soaking or a share of whole bunches, fermented warm, and aged in barrique, new or used according to the site; a lighter village style is still made for local drinking, and the old pale, slightly sweet Baden Pinot is now a memory. Grauburgunder and Weissburgunder are fermented dry, in stainless steel for freshness or in large and small oak with lees contact for weight, and Chardonnay is handled the same way. Gutedel is kept simple and bottled early. Weissherbst, a single variety rosé, and Badisch Rotgold, a Rotling of Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder fermented together, are the region's pink traditions. Sekt by the traditional method from the Pinot family is a Baden strength. Tauberfranken and the Neuweier vineyards near Baden-Baden may use the Bocksbeutel flask that is otherwise Franken's.

law.classification: Baden is one of the thirteen Anbaugebiete, so its Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein carry the name and a test number, ranked by must weight from Qualitätswein through the Prädikat ladder, with the 2021 origin pyramid of Anbaugebiet, Region, Ort and Einzellage over it and Erstes Gewächs and Grosses Gewächs as protected dry single site terms, binding in full from the 2026 vintage. Baden alone sits in European wine zone B, so enrichment of the must is capped at a lower level than in the zone A regions. It has nine Bereiche from north to south: Tauberfranken, Badische Bergstrasse, Kraichgau, Ortenau, Breisgau, Kaiserstuhl, Tuniberg, Markgräflerland and Bodensee. Badisch Rotgold is a protected Rotling and the Bocksbeutel is allowed in Tauberfranken and around Neuweier. Within the VDP's pyramid, Baden's Grosses Gewächs list is broad by German standards, with Spätburgunder, Weissburgunder, Grauburgunder and Riesling among its grapes.
tiers: The protected geographical indication level, here Badischer Landwein.
Quality wine from Baden alone, test number required; enrichment allowed only within the lower zone B limit.
Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese by must weight at picking, never enriched; in Baden the lower Prädikat wines are mostly fermented dry.

Protected terms for dry wine of protected origin from a named single vineyard: the ordinance caps Erstes Gewächs at 60 hectolitres per hectare, 70 on steep slopes, and holds Grosses Gewächs to a lower cap, hand picking and a later release.
The association's top site class; a Baden GG may be Spätburgunder, Weissburgunder, Grauburgunder or Riesling, among others.
labels: Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris and Pinot Blanc; the family that defines Baden.
Pinot Gris in the older, richer, often sweeter style; Grauburgunder signals dry.
The Ortenau's name for Riesling, from the Klingelberg site at Durbach.
In the Ortenau, Traminer; the same word means Frühburgunder elsewhere, so read the region.
A rosé from one named red variety, Qualitätswein or above.
A protected Baden Rotling of Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder fermented together.
Permitted in Baden only for Tauberfranken and the Neuweier vineyards.
Legally dry, at most 4 grams per litre of sugar or up to 9 where acidity is within 2 grams of it.

places.name: Kaiserstuhl
places.note: An extinct volcano rising out of the Rhine plain north west of Freiburg, capped with deep loess and cut into terraces, the warmest vineyard in Germany. Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder from its volcanic rock are the region's most famous wines, and its villages hold its leading estates and the great cooperative at Breisach.

places.name: Ihringen
places.note: The village with the Winklerberg, a steep volcanic site on the south west flank, long counted Germany's hottest vineyard; Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder of smoke and spice.

places.name: Achkarren
places.note: A village on the south side whose Schlossberg of volcanic rock gives firm Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder.

places.name: Oberrotweil and Burkheim
places.note: Villages of the western Kaiserstuhl with sites such as Henkenberg, Eichberg and Feuerberg, strong in Spätburgunder from loess and volcanic ground.

places.name: Oberbergen and Bickensohl
places.note: Inner Kaiserstuhl villages; Oberbergen's Bassgeige is known for Pinot Noir and Pinot Gris.

places.name: Tuniberg
places.note: A low loess hill beside the Kaiserstuhl towards Freiburg, without the volcanic core, giving softer Spätburgunder and Pinot whites.

places.name: Breisgau
places.note: The foothills north of Freiburg towards Lahr, on limestone, marl and loess. Malterdingen, whose name once stood for the Pinot Noir grape itself, is the home of Baden's reference Spätburgunder estate.

places.name: Malterdingen
places.note: A limestone village whose Bienenberg and neighbouring sites give structured, Burgundian Spätburgunder and Chardonnay; not in the Kaiserstuhl, a common slip.

places.name: Ortenau
places.note: The foothills between Offenburg and Baden-Baden, on granite and gneiss. Riesling, called Klingelberger here, and Spätburgunder are its wines; Durbach is its best known village and Neuweier its Bocksbeutel enclave.

places.name: Durbach
places.note: A steep granite village with the Plauelrain and Schloss Staufenberg; Riesling as Klingelberger, Traminer as Clevner and firm Spätburgunder.

places.name: Neuweier
places.note: A village near Baden-Baden whose Riesling is sold in the Bocksbeutel under a historic exception.

places.name: Markgräflerland
places.note: The southern end of the region between Freiburg and Basel, on limestone and loess, the home of Gutedel, which the Margrave of Baden brought from Vevey in 1780. Spätburgunder and the Pinot whites have grown in standing beside it.

places.name: Efringen-Kirchen and the Isteiner Klotz
places.note: Limestone sites near Basel where serious Spätburgunder and Gutedel are made against the Swiss border.

places.name: Bodensee
places.note: The Lake Constance outpost around Meersburg, among the highest vineyards in Germany; Spätburgunder Weissherbst and Müller-Thurgau on moraine, with the lake storing light and warmth.

places.name: Kraichgau
places.note: Rolling loess hills between Karlsruhe and Heidelberg, with the Pinot family, Riesling and Lemberger from a scatter of estates.

places.name: Badische Bergstrasse
places.note: The Baden stretch of the old road below the Odenwald around Heidelberg; a Bereich of Baden, while the Hessian stretch is a region of its own.

places.name: Tauberfranken
places.note: The northern outpost on the Tauber, Muschelkalk and Silvaner country that tastes of Franken and may use the Bocksbeutel.

producers.name: Bernhard Huber
producers.why: The Malterdingen estate that set the standard for Burgundian Spätburgunder in Germany, on Breisgau limestone.

producers.name: Dr. Heger
producers.why: Ihringen house whose Winklerberg Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder define the volcanic Kaiserstuhl.

producers.name: Franz Keller
producers.why: Oberbergen estate with the Schwarzer Adler restaurant, a pioneer of dry Baden Pinot in the French manner.

producers.name: Salwey
producers.why: Oberrotweil estate for taut Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder from the western Kaiserstuhl.

producers.name: Bercher
producers.why: Burkheim family house whose Feuerberg Spätburgunder and Weissburgunder are Kaiserstuhl classics.

producers.name: Laible
producers.why: Durbach estate that made the Ortenau's granite Riesling, Klingelberger, a national reference.

producers.name: Ziereisen
producers.why: Markgräflerland grower near Basel known for site driven Spätburgunder and serious Gutedel.

producers.name: Schloss Neuweier
producers.why: The Neuweier estate whose Riesling in the Bocksbeutel is the Baden exception every student must know.

producers.name: Stigler
producers.why: Ihringen house with historic Winklerberg terraces and long aged Spätburgunder.

producers.name: Badischer Winzerkeller
producers.why: The Breisach cooperative, among the largest in Europe, which makes a great share of Baden's wine.

producers.name: Markgraf von Baden
producers.why: The margrave's estates at Salem on the Bodensee and Staufenberg in the Ortenau, a historic name across two Bereiche.

exam: Place Baden: the Rhine's eastern bank from Lake Constance to Heidelberg, facing Alsace, with the Tauber outpost in the north.
Say the signature: Germany's warmest region, zone B alone, Pinot family country, Spätburgunder first.
Know the Kaiserstuhl as an extinct volcano capped with loess terraces, the hottest vineyard in Germany.
Name the nine Bereiche and attach a grape to each of the main ones: Ortenau Riesling, Markgräflerland Gutedel, Kaiserstuhl Pinot.
Decode Grauburgunder, Ruländer, Weissburgunder, Klingelberger and Clevner.
Know Weissherbst and Badisch Rotgold, and where the Bocksbeutel is allowed in Baden.
Know the VDP's Baden GG list, broad by German standards, and Malterdingen as the Spätburgunder reference.
traps: Baden is the warmest German region and the only one in zone B, so it may enrich less, not more.
Malterdingen is in the Breisgau, not the Kaiserstuhl.
Grauburgunder and Ruländer are both Pinot Gris; the first signals dry, the second richer and often sweeter.
Clevner means Traminer in the Ortenau but Frühburgunder in Württemberg; read the region before answering.
Badisch Rotgold is a co-fermented Rotling of two grapes; Weissherbst is a rosé of one.
The Badische Bergstrasse is a Bereich of Baden; the Hessische Bergstrasse is a separate Anbaugebiet.
Baden's Riesling is a speciality of the Ortenau, not the region's lead grape.

cards.f: Baden in one line
cards.b: Germany's southernmost, warmest region, zone B alone, from Lake Constance up the Rhine to Heidelberg: Pinot family country, Spätburgunder first, cooperatives making most of it.

cards.f: What is the Kaiserstuhl?
cards.b: An extinct volcano in the Rhine plain near Freiburg, capped with loess and cut into terraces; Germany's hottest vineyard, for Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder.

cards.f: The nine Bereiche of Baden, north to south
cards.b: Tauberfranken, Badische Bergstrasse, Kraichgau, Ortenau, Breisgau, Kaiserstuhl, Tuniberg, Markgräflerland, Bodensee.

cards.f: Grape by Bereich: Ortenau, Markgräflerland, Kaiserstuhl
cards.b: Ortenau: Riesling (Klingelberger) on granite. Markgräflerland: Gutedel (Chasselas). Kaiserstuhl: Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder on volcanic rock and loess.

cards.f: Grauburgunder versus Ruländer
cards.b: Both are Pinot Gris. Grauburgunder signals the dry style; Ruländer the older, richer, often sweeter one.

cards.f: Weissherbst versus Badisch Rotgold
cards.b: Weissherbst: a rosé from one named red grape. Badisch Rotgold: a protected Baden Rotling, Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder fermented together.

cards.f: Where in Baden may the Bocksbeutel be used?
cards.b: Tauberfranken in the north and the Neuweier vineyards near Baden-Baden in the Ortenau.

cards.f: Why does zone B matter for Baden?
cards.b: Baden is the only German region in EU zone B, so its permitted enrichment is lower (2 per cent by volume against 3 in zone A): the sun does the work.

cards.f: Which grapes lead Baden's VDP Grosses Gewächs list?
cards.b: Spätburgunder, Weissburgunder and Grauburgunder, with Riesling in the Ortenau: one of the broadest lists in Germany.

questions.q: Baden alone among Germany's thirteen regions is placed in a warmer European wine growing zone. Which zone?
questions.exp: The other twelve regions sit in zone A, the coolest. Zone B holds Baden with much of northern France, and it caps enrichment of the must at a lower level because the climate ripens the grapes itself.

questions.q: An extinct volcano rising from the Rhine plain near Freiburg, capped with loess terraces, is Baden's hottest and most famous vineyard area. Name it.
questions.exp: The Kaiserstuhl's volcanic rock under deep loess records the highest temperatures in German viticulture. Ihringen, Achkarren, Oberrotweil and Burkheim are its leading villages, planted to Spätburgunder and Grauburgunder.

questions.q: Which grape, known as Chasselas in Switzerland, is the speciality of the Markgräflerland in the far south of Baden?
questions.exp: Gutedel was brought to the Markgräflerland from Vevey in 1780 and gives a soft, low acid wine drunk young. Elbling is the Obermosel's grape, Silvaner belongs to Franken and Tauberfranken, and Müller-Thurgau is grown across Baden for volume.

questions.q: Klingelberger appears on labels from Durbach in the Ortenau. Which grape is it?
questions.exp: Klingelberger is the Ortenau's traditional name for Riesling, taken from the Klingelberg vineyard at Durbach. Traminer is called Clevner in the same villages, and Pinot Gris is Grauburgunder or Ruländer.

questions.q: Baden's own Rotling, Grauburgunder and Spätburgunder fermented together, carries a protected name. What is it?
questions.exp: Badisch Rotgold must be a Qualitätswein made by co-fermenting the two Pinot grapes, which separates it from a Weissherbst, the single variety rosé. Württemberg's equivalent Rotling is Schillerwein.

questions.q: Malterdingen, home of Baden's reference Spätburgunder estate, lies in which Bereich?
questions.exp: Malterdingen sits on limestone in the Breisgau, the foothills north of Freiburg, and its name was once used for the Pinot Noir grape itself. Students routinely misplace it in the Kaiserstuhl.

questions.q: Which northern Bereich of Baden, on Muschelkalk and planted to Silvaner, is allowed to use the Bocksbeutel?
questions.exp: Tauberfranken on the river Tauber tastes and bottles like Franken, and shares the flask's protection with the Neuweier vineyards near Baden-Baden. The Kraichgau and Bergstrasse are loess hill country and the Bodensee is the lake outpost in the south.

questions.q: What covers the volcanic rock on the terraced slopes of the Kaiserstuhl?
questions.exp: Deep wind blown loess was laid over the volcano during the ice ages and holds both water and warmth. Slate belongs to the Mosel and Ahr, granite to the Ortenau foothills and Muschelkalk to Franken and Tauberfranken.
